item.title: [CBS Sports] The state of the outfield position heading into 2027: Pete Crow-Armstrong leads a talented but thin field

item.content:encoded:
There were 13 outfield-eligible players worth at least $20 in the FanGraphs Player Rater in 2026, just two fewer than the first base spot. If you remember that you only need to start one first baseman (and potentially a corner infielder and DH) while you might need to start as many as five outfielders at a time, well, you can see why this is problematic.
That's not to say the outfield is somehow a wasteland for Fantasy right now. First base was unusually strong in 2026, but in 2025, there were three times as many $20 players with outfield eligibility as at first base. And it's worth noting that the 13 $20 outfielders in 2026 are actually a few more than 2025's nine.
On the whole, I look at outfield as a position with a decent amount of depth in a three-outfielder, 12-team league. You should be able to draft a full lineup without feeling too bad about your outfield options in that formula.
Once you start getting into five-outfielder leagues, and especially deeper leagues with 15 teams, it starts to feel a lot more thin. That's to be expected, of course, but it's important to keep that in mind when you're preparing for the 2027 season. You don't have to make the position a priority in every draft, but if you aren't cognizant of it, you could end up with a real weakness in those deeper leagues.
For more on the state of the outfield position, .
2026 Outfield Review
- Pete Crow-Armstrong, CHC: .280 - 119 - 45 - 107 - 41
- Yordan Alvarez, HOU: .316 - 105 - 42 - 106 - 1
- Fernando Tatis Jr., SDP: .289 - 96 - 25 - 83 - 38
- Randy Arozarena, SEA: .281 - 113 - 26 - 79 - 26
- Jordan Walker, STL: .269 - 97 - 29 - 102 - 22
- James Wood, WSN: .265 - 106 - 30 - 77 - 21
- Jackson Chourio, MIL: .291 - 96 - 25 - 75 - 23
- Alec Burleson, STL: .279 - 89 - 26 - 116 - 4
- Jake McCarthy, COL: .291 - 80 - 15 - 83 - 32
- Michael Harris II, ATL: .294 - 79 - 26 - 87 - 12
- Jackson Merrill, SDP: .254 - 86 - 26 - 87 - 27
- Bryce Harper, PHI: .269 - 93 - 29 - 87 - 7
- Jake Bauers, MIL: .266 - 93 - 26 - 86 - 11
- Seiya Suzuki, CHC: .270 - 96 - 26 - 86 - 3
- Carson Benge, NYM: .282 - 86 - 20 - 65 - 22
- Andy Pages, LAD: .274 - 75 - 23 - 85 - 13
- Corbin Carroll, ARI: .239 - 91 - 22 - 78 - 21
- Oneil Cruz, PIT: .280 - 65 - 20 - 67 - 30
- Daylen Lile, WSN: .246 - 81 - 22 - 89 - 15
- Jac Caglianone, KCR: .289 - 72 - 23 - 75 - 7
- Bryan Reynolds, PIT: .261 - 102 - 17 - 72 - 9
- Chandler Simpson, TBR: .306 - 66 - 0 - 38 - 46
- Riley Greene, DET: .280 - 79 - 21 - 75 - 3
- Ceddanne Rafaela, BOS: .285 - 67 - 16 - 70 - 17
"Marginal player signs with the Rockies and has a Coors Field-inflated career season" used to be a pretty reliable archetype. Still, the Rockies have given Fantasy players little to get excited about in recent years. Jake McCarthy stands out as a notable exception, as his contact-and-speed profile proved to be a perfect fit for Coos Field. We're talking about relatively easy career-best production across the board, in a way that feels relatively obvious in retrospect. I don't have a ton of faith that this would prove replicable in any other ballpark — the gap between his .321 expected wOBA and his .349 actual mark was the 20th biggest in baseball — but it works there. As long as he isn't traded, McCarthy is a good bet to replicate his 2026 success.
I also want to highlight Harris and Merrill, because it feels very natural to group them together. They're both younger than you might realize – Harris will turn 26 shortly before his sixth MLB season in March, while Merrill won't even be 24 on Opening Day. They're also both linked by the combination of plus athleticism and bat speed, plus pretty poor approaches at the plate. They are, on the whole, capable of overcoming their poor swing decisions with outlier outcomes when they make contact, but that isn't always the case for either. Hence, the lengthy slumps that have held both back in recent years. They both got the good end of their range of outcomes in 2026, and we saw how high the ceiling can be for both. But drafting either for their 2026 outcome will carry inherent risks until they show some growth in their plate discipline.
Biggest Breakout from 2026
Pete Crow-Armstrong, Cubs
How could it be anyone else? Crow-Armstrong went from being a talented but deeply flawed hitter to arguably the best player in baseball, and he did it in-season. Early on, he looked more or less like the same guy he had always been, walking just nine times in 128 plate appearances through the end of June; he walked at least 12 times in each of the final five months of the season, something he had never done in any of his previous 13 months. He did that without sacrificing the pull-side power that has long been a key part of his game, and it turned him into one of the most dominant hitters in the game. Expecting all of those gains to carry over into 2027 might be asking a bit much — sometimes guys just get super locked in for a while — but he's clearly a much-improved hitter, and one who should be the first player taken in every single Roto league in 2027. And he shouldn't go much later in points leagues, where he was also the top player in 2026.
Honorable Mention: Jordan Walker, Cardinals
Okay, so if it were going to be anyone but Crow-Armstrong, it would be Walker, who went from being one of the biggest prospect busts in recent seasons to one of the best players in Fantasy. Walker still had pretty bad plate discipline and swing-and-miss issues, but he overcame that by being more aggressive early in the count and by doing more damage when he did make contact. The plate discipline issues and a late-season swoon — his expected wOBA dropped from .374 to .290 from the first half to the second — hint at the kind of risk involved in buying fully into what he did in 2026, and I suspect I'll be a little lower on him than the consensus. On the other hand, those were the exact reasons I cited to avoid Crow-Armstrong before the season, and look how that turned out. There's something to be said for just betting on the young, super-talented players when they show it.
Biggest Bust from 2026
The overall numbers don't show it, but Judge looked more or less like himself before he started dealing with that rib injury. In March and April, he posted a .450 xwOBA, right in line with his typical mark, but then things went downhill even before he ultimately went on the IL with a fractured rib. Was his downturn because of the injury? If so, then I think you can still make the case for him as a top-five pick in any league. But we're talking about a guy who will be 35 early next season, coming off a largely lost season that also came with an apparent decline in the underlying skill level, and that's a lot of red flags to overlook in a top-five pick. I might end up with Judge ranked that way come the spring, but it won't feel good.
Honorable Mention: Kyle Tucker, Dodgers
Maybe you don't think he was worth the contract the Dodgers gave him. Fair enough; you won't be alone in holding that opinion. But anyone who tells you there was any way to see this kind of disaster coming from Tucker is just lying to you. A 29-year-old went out and posted the worst batting average, on-base percentage, and slugging percentage of his career, and in two of those cases, it wasn't even close. Tucker had the combination of bat speed, athleticism, and plate discipline that should protect him against this kind of drop-off. Maybe the lights in L.A. were too bright for him. Maybe the pressure of the contract got to him. But I don't believe Tucker has just completely lost the ability to be an impact player, and he's still in what should be one of the best lineups in baseball, so I'll buy the bounce-back at what should be a steeply discounted price. The fact that he put together an excellent September and a very good postseason run certainly makes that an easier story to tell, of course.
Biggest rankings movers from 2026 to 2027
Up: Pete Crow-Armstrong, Cubs; Yordan Alvarez, Astros; Jordan Walker, Cardinals; Jake Bauers, Brewers
As maybe the biggest Yordan Alvarez believer in the entire Fantasy industry coming into 2026, I do worry there's going to be a big overcorrection on him in 2027. We didn't learn anything new about Alvarez. If you think 2026 was a breakout season of some sort for him, I'm sorry, but you just weren't paying attention; he's just always been this good. His .442 xwOBA was higher than his career average, sure, but it was also not even the highest of his career, and he had a separate season with a .436 mark, too. The skills have always been there, but the difference is that he stayed healthy in 2026 after a bunch of injuries in previous seasons. I'm thrilled that he stayed healthy, and the fact that he did it in a season when his standing among Fantasy players was never lower is a good reminder that the Fantasy community isn't nearly as good at predicting who will and won't stay healthy as we think. But that will also be true in 2027: He'll be a top-five pick in most leagues despite the injury risk not being substantially different than it was last season. That's not to say he shouldn't be a top-five pick, of course; it's to say that he should have been a lot closer to a top-five pick last season than he was.
You could make a case for Bauers as the biggest breakout at outfield, because he was viewed as an even bigger afterthought than Walker was. He was a 30-year-old platoon specialist, after all! That he somehow went out in 2026 and put up a .901 OPS against lefties and had the best season of his career by a mile came completely out of nowhere, and it's going to be very interesting to see what the market for him as a free agent looks like this offseason. I buy a lot of what he did in 2026, and I suspect there will be enough skepticism around it to keep his price pretty reasonable. But betting on age-30 breakouts is historically a pretty bad idea, so you'll have to get a pretty big discount on what he did in 2026 to make him worth the risk, I think.
Down: Ronald Acuna, Braves; Kyle Tucker, Dodgers; Wyatt Langford, Rangers; Brent Rooker, Athletics
I wanted to make Langford one of the biggest bust picks, if only to highlight the fact that he has almost certainly been the least profitable pick in Fantasy over the past three years. He has struggled to stay healthy and just hasn't been the impact player you'd expect from a guy who had the kind of prospect pedigree he did — not to mention the benefit of the doubt the Fantasy community has continued to give him. I suspect that will come to an end in 2027, and … it kind of makes me more excited about buying into him this season. Because, for as frustrating and disappointing as he's been as a big-leaguer, his per-162 game pace for his career is pretty terrific: 90 runs, 24 homers, 24 steals, and 77 RBI. If he just does that in 2027, isn't that worth something like a fifth-round pick? And I don't think that's the ceiling for Langford, who has put up those numbers at a very young age while playing through a variety of injuries and has certainly flashed a higher ceiling at times. I'm not trying to excuse his poor performance; I'm just pointing out that all he has to do is stay healthy to be a very good Fantasy option. That's usually a good player to buy into at a discount.
The notoriously frugal A's are surely feeling some degree of buyer's remorse on Rooker's contract, but that contract should assure that he continues to play every day for them. His disappointing season came to an end after just 48 games, but he was on pace for another 30-homer season despite the injury. The .200 average is a tough look, as was the career-worst 32% strikeout rate, and the big drop off as a 31-year-old will rightly lead to plenty of skepticism around the potential of a bounce back. But that will also mean Rooker will come at a huge discount, potentially with a price outside the top 200 in many drafts. I'll buy that dip, personally. If you can buy him as a very cheap bench bat, there's no downside.
Offseason preview
Who needs an upgrade most?
A bunch of these teams are straddling the line between trying to go for it and needing to rebuild. The Reds could very well be in the market for a big upgrade in the outfield, or they could decide to move Elly De La Cruz and hit the reset button (again). The Astros could decide to give it one more run with this core, or they could move Alvarez and pivot to the future. The Phillies seem most likely to try to take a big swing, if only because Dave Dombrowski only knows how to take big swings. However, the Cardinals loom as a team that is ascending and could decide to get involved in the free-agent market with their core of cost-controlled position players.
Top impending free agents
- Randy Arozarena
- Seiya Suzuki
- Ian Happ
- Jake Bauers
- Trent Grisham
- Daulton Varsho
- Luis Robert
- Ramon Laureano
- George Springer
Arozarena is such a fascinating free agent. He's coming off a perfectly timed career-best season, but he'll be 32 before Opening Day and has rated out as a pretty terrible defender for several years running. There's probably no chance he gets anything more than a five-year contract in free agency, and he might need to agree to a move to DH as soon as 2027, two things that might be a tough pill to swallow. But having the best season of his career in the toughest offensive environment in baseball is no small thing, and nobody can deny his flair for the dramatic would be a great fit for a team with championship aspirations. The underlying skill set doesn't look so different from previous seasons, but his price will likely be higher than ever, making him one of the more obvious players to avoid in drafts for 2027, no matter where he lands.
Suzuki and, to a lesser extent, Happ look like players who will carry pretty solid value in Fantasy no matter where they land, but everyone else looks pretty context-dependent. Varsho's pull-heavy swing (and elite center field defense) would be a perfect fit for the Yankees, for example, but would be a much less interesting profile elsewhere. Stay tuned.
Trade candidates 
- Yordan Alvarez, Astros
- Jarren Duran, Red Sox
- Steven Kwan, Guardians
- Byron Buxton, Twins
- Brent Rooker, Athletics
- Jake McCarthy, Rockies
Alvarez feels like the biggest wild card here. The Astros won the AL West, but with just a .500 record, and they had such a poor showing in a two-game Wild Card round loss to the White Sox that the hometown crowd showered them with boos along the way. The Astros have lost their long-held edge over the competition, and while Alvarez's contract isn't expiring, he only has two years left on a relatively below-market deal. So this might be their last chance to maximize their return for him. The Astros are in flux in a lot of ways after firing Dana Brown, so they might not be positioned to make a big, franchise-altering move, but they would probably be best served trying to get off the treadmill of mediocrity sooner rather than later.
It increasingly looks like the Red Sox should have traded Duran at least a year ago, if not longer. All of a sudden, he's a 30-year-old corner outfielder who probably shouldn't play every day against lefties, and while he'll likely still earn a below-market salary in arbitration, he no longer looks like a real bargain. His skill set still has plenty of value for Fantasy (20 homers, 21 steals will always play), and I'd bet on him improving on last year's .207 average, but this isn't an early-round profile anymore.
Top rookies to know for 2026
- Josue De Paula, Dodgers
- Walker Jenkins, Twins
- Eduardo Quintero, Dodgers
- Theo Gillen, Rays
- Mike Sirota, Dodgers
- Zyhir Hope, Tigers
- Edward Florentino, Pirates
- Eric Hartman, Braves
- Drew Burress, Athletics
- Josiah Hartshorn, Cubs
- Lazaro Montes, Mariners
Jenkins is probably the most likely player here to be in an Opening Day lineup – I'm not sure what would have to happen for him not to be there, absent injury. He didn't take the league by storm in his first 26 games, but he was actually pretty great once he got adjusted, hitting .385/.400/.615 with just three strikeouts over his final 10 games. He has power, speed, and an excellent approach at the plate and should be a popular breakout candidate for 2027.
But not as popular as De Paula could be. I say "could" because, well, there's no obvious place for him to play. It's definitely not going to be in right field or DH, and slotting De Paula in at left field would require finding somewhere for Teoscar Hernandez and his large salary to go. Center field is the biggest hole in the Yankees outfield, but De Paula hasn't played there since 2023, and … well, you see the problem here. De Paula destroyed Double-A and very much passed the eye test in 11 MLB games, earning not-totally-unfair comparisons to Juan Soto and Yordan Alvarez for his approach at the plate. He could be an absolute star, but given the roster crunch and the fact that he's only 21 and hasn't played at Triple-A yet, this might be a situation like Junior Caminero's a few years back – remember, he debuted toward the end of the 2023 season but wasn't an everyday player until August of 2024. I hope it doesn't take that long, but we'll have to at least consider the possibility that it will.

item.content:encoded:
Former Minnesota Twins president of baseball and business operations Derek Falvey “mutually parted ways” last spring and one of the underlying storylines of this season has been where he would end up. Taking the season to evaluate the landscape, we may have finally found our answer as The Athletic’s Ken Rosenthal and Will Sammon reported on Wednesday that Falvey will be joining the New York Mets front office under lead executive David Sterns.
At first glance, this looks like a perfect landing spot for Falvey. While we don’t know the exact reason why Falvey abruptly resigned in February, a good bet was that he was tired of the tightening purse strings from the Pohlad family when they slashed the team’s payroll in 2023 and 2024 before he orchestrated a fire sale ahead of the 2025 trade deadline. The Mets won’t have that problem as Steve Cohen is one of baseball’s most free-spending owners West of Los Angeles, but it may not have been Falvey’s biggest issue.
Instead, more money could be an even bigger problem for Falvey and while his role is undefined, there’s enough evidence to suggest that he could put the Mets in a deeper hole as he begins his next chapter.
Derek Falvey’s biggest problem with the Twins wasn’t a lack of money
The Twins hired Falvey in 2017 as a way to reboot their franchise. Terry Ryan was one of the greatest general managers in team history during their rise in the 2000s, but upon his return in 2011, his methods had gotten old and stale, resulting in what former Twins chairman Jim Pohlad called a “total system failure.”
For a team that had traditionally looked within the organization to hire managers and front office personnel, plucking Falvey from the Cleveland Guardians felt like a massive victory. The Guardians had done more with less throughout the 2010s, including a trip to the World Series in 2016, and his knack for developing pitching also convinced the Twins to bring him aboard as the executive vice president and chief baseball officer.
Falvey’s tenure came with some immediate hits, hiring manager Rocco Baldelli and signing Nelson Cruz as a free agent to spark the “Bomba Squad” team that won 101 games and set an MLB record with 307 home runs in 2019. He also signed Max Kepler and Jorge Polanco to cost-controlled, long-term extensions and made a pair of shrewd trades that brought Joe Ryan for Cruz in 2021 and Pablo López for Luis Arraez in 2023.
But even with the good moves, Falvey wasn’t at his best when he spent money. The 2018 offseason was a disaster as Falvey signed Lance Lynn, Logan Morrison and Addison Reed to a combined $35.25 million. In 2020, he signed Josh Donaldson to a four-year, $92 million contract. In 2021, he signed Alex Colomé to a one-year, $6.25 million contract to watch him post a 4.15 ERA and after wisely signing Carlos Correa in 2022, he handed out a six-year, $200 million contract the following offseason after the Mets and the San Francisco Giants backed out of mega-deals over long-term health concerns.
These contracts emphasized some of the other poor decisions Falvey made over the years. While Hunter Greene has had arm problems this season, his performance during the 2024 and 2025 seasons (16-9, 2.76 ERA) suggests he would have been a better choice than Royce Lewis with the No. 1 overall pick in the 2017 MLB Draft.
The 2022 trade deadline was another disaster as Falvey traded for Tyler Mahle and Jorge López only to have both pitchers flame out within a calendar year. The trade for Chris Paddack before the 2022 season sent out a future All-Star in Brent Rooker and the Twins only won one playoff series during his nine seasons with the team.
The Twins left the Mets a warning about Derek Falvey
Falvey’s overall resume is likely what’s appealing to the Mets and they could use some new voices after a disappointing year. After spending $359.2 million in payroll this season per Cot’s Baseball Contracts, New York is currently last in the National League East with a 73-85 record. Their roster is filled with contracts that would make Falvey blush from his time with the Twins. But if they’re expecting him to solve their issues, they should look at the mess he left behind in Minnesota.
The Twins lineup is filled with players that Falvey drafted but never reached their potential. Lewis is the headliner, but others such as Trevor Larnach and Matt Wallner have turned out to be below-average players with Wallner still stuck in the minor leagues.
Falvey’s final free agent signings also didn’t turn out well. While Josh Bell had a solid season, hitting .255/.317/.416 with 20 homers and 92 RBI, Victor Caratini looks like a similar mistake to Christian Vazquez’s three-year, $30 million contract in 2023.
The lack of starting pitching, something that was regarded as a calling card for Falvey coming over from the Guardians, was also glaring as the Twins scrambled to fill roles with Zebby Matthews and Connor Prielipp.
Even one of Falvey’s worst trades as general manager haunted this year’s team as Austin Martin posted an OPS+ of 88 (100 is league average) and Simeon Woods Richardson didn’t make it to June after being acquired in the 2022 trade that sent Jose Berríos to the Toronto Blue Jays.
With that, bringing in Falvey to try and solve the issues the Mets have feels a lot like his promotion to the president of baseball and business operations ahead of the 2025 season. Falvey won’t have as much power in New York, but it also could dispel the theory that giving him some more money to throw at his problems won’t magically turn him into a competent executive.

item.content:encoded:
We’re down to the final days of the 2026 regular season with still quite a number of teams that have something to play for -- including a few who are fighting for their postseason lives.
Such is the case with the Astros and Rangers, who are tied atop the AL West (with Houston owning the tiebreaker); the team that loses the division will most likely miss the playoffs entirely. Elsewhere in the American League, the Guardians and White Sox are still battling for the division title, though the loser of that should slot into the third wild-card spot.
While all the divisions in the National League have been clinched already, the wild-card race, specifically in terms of seeding, is very much heating up, with the Phillies, Cubs and Padres entering play on Wednesday in a three-way tie.
Which clubs will get to keep playing into October? And which will watch their playoff aspirations come to an end?
Our expert panel has ranked every team based on a combination of what we’ve seen so far and what we already knew going into the 162-game marathon that is a full baseball season. We also asked ESPN MLB experts Bradford Doolittle, Buster Olney and Jorge Castillo to weigh in with an observation for all 30 teams.
1. Milwaukee Brewers
Record: 99-59
Previous ranking: 1
With the season down to a handful of games, the Brewers have all but run out of time for Kyle Harrison to recover his first-half form. Harrison was 8-2 with a 3.01 ERA before the break; he’s 2-3 with a 7.80 ERA since. His strikeout rate has remained steady, even as his velocity and movement measures have become more volatile. Meanwhile, his walk rate has more than doubled, and his homers-allowed rate has nearly tripled. Suffice to say, this is not a great combination of trends. Milwaukee has tried to get Harrison back in stride by using him out of the bullpen, but he’s gotten hammered as a reliever. Brewers fans who dreamed of a big three rotation of Jacob Misiorowski, Harrison and Logan Henderson probably need to recalibrate their expectations at this point. -- Doolittle
2. Los Angeles Dodgers
Record: 97-61
Previous ranking: 2
We’re nearing October baseball, and it’s as if the Dodgers are knocking off items on a to-do list. Shohei Ohtani back in the lineup? Check. Edwin Diaz finding his stuff, finally? Check. Will Smith back in the lineup? Check -- and he has an OPS of close to 1.000 this month. Mookie Betts back to being Mookie Betts? Check. Kyle Tucker digging out of his seasonlong slump? Check. L.A. is putting the pieces back together just in time as it begins its effort to become the first NL team to go back-to-back-to-back. -- Olney
3. Tampa Bay Rays
Record: 96-62
Previous ranking: 3
Tampa Bay began the season with the longest odds to win the AL East. On Tuesday, it clinched its first division title since 2021 with a win over the Yankees. The Rays will enter their first postseason since 2023 as the favorites to win the AL pennant behind a distinct home-field advantage at Tropicana Field, a strong pitching staff and a dynamic lineup centered around MVP candidate Junior Caminero, designated hitter Yandy Diaz and first baseman Jonathan Aranda. With a payroll that ranks 28th in the majors, the Rays seek to become the team with the lowest-ranked payroll to ever win the World Series. -- Castillo
4. Atlanta Braves
Record: 93-65
Previous ranking: 5
Atlanta would’ve preferred to get a first-round bye in the playoffs, of course, but the fact that the Brewers and Dodgers seemed to have locked down the No. 1 and No. 2 seeds allows the Braves to treat this last week of the regular season like the last week of spring training. They can plot out the best way to rest their key relievers, assess the progress of Robert Suarez and arrange at-bats for the position players to be primed for the postseason. Meanwhile, the teams the Braves are likely to face in the first round -- the Phillies, Cubs and Padres -- are all still pushing for berths and home-field advantage in the wild-card round. -- Olney
5. New York Yankees
Record: 91-67
Previous ranking: 4
Despite manager Aaron Boone saying on Tuesday that Aaron Judge isn’t expected to return from his calf strain in time for the wild-card round, Judge told ESPN the following day that he does in fact intend to be ready for Game 1. He suffered the injury last Wednesday and was placed on the injured list two days later. The Yankees were initially cryptic about the setback, declining to disclose the severity and Judge’s outlook.
Boone offered some clarity Tuesday when he called it a “moderate strain” and acknowledged that the club does not plan on having him to open the postseason. Judge received a PPP injection Monday. The Yankees hope that will spur recovery. Otherwise, New York faces an uphill challenge to survive in October without its three-time MVP at his best. -- Castillo
6. Chicago Cubs
Record: 87-71
Previous ranking: 6
No player has made more of a second-half leap than Alex Bregman, whose season has just gathered momentum almost daily since the last week of July. That momentum was stopped in its tracks when Bregman suffered facial fractures last weekend when struck by a foul ball. The good news is that the Cubs decided against placing Bregman on the IL, believing he might be ready for the playoffs after.
But even if that proves to be optimistic, Cubs fans can take solace in the presence of icy-cool rookie Pedro Ramirez. The Cubs didn’t drop off much when Dansby Swanson was injured, as Ramirez provided a league-average bat and glove work at both second and third base that has kept an elite Cubs defense on track. You want Bregman in there, for sure -- but Ramirez provides a heck of a Plan B. -- Doolittle
7. San Diego Padres
Record: 88-70
Previous ranking: 8
San Diego’s magic number for clinching a playoff spot is shrinking, allowing general manager A.J. Preller and skipper Craig Stammen the chance to line up their staff for the wild-card series, with options developing. Stammen indicated to reporters that unless Michael King is needed to clinch a playoff spot on the last day of the regular season, he will be held over to start Game 1 of the wild card, wherever that is -- so he wouldn’t necessarily be used Sunday in order to win home-field advantage in the first round of the playoffs.
Additionally, the Padres are in a better position to rest their bullpen, the perceived strength of the team. Adrian Morejon ranks third among all relievers in innings. Rest might be overrated for Mason Miller: He has made 16 appearances on zero days’ rest, and in those games, he has allowed two hits and one earned run in 16⅔ innings, with two walks and 27 strikeouts. -- Olney
8. Philadelphia Phillies
Record: 87-71
Previous ranking: 7
The culture of Philadelphia’s starting pitchers, from Zack Wheeler to Cristopher Sanchez to Aaron Nola, is to pitch deep into games. Unlike so many starters in this generation, Wheeler takes the mound expecting to work into the late innings -- and the Phillies will need this sort of production from the rotation, given the team’s recent bullpen problems. Orion Kerkering, an important part of the relief corps, struggled so badly that he was sent to the minors last week. Jose Alvarado has pitched better down the stretch, and hard-throwing Alex MacFarlane has quickly ascended into an important role in his rookie season in the bullpen. But the Phillies’ rotation will carry the team’s October dreams. -- Olney
9. Boston Red Sox
Record: 85-73
Previous ranking: 9
The Red Sox rewarded Chad Tracy on Tuesday for leading the team’s historic turnaround by removing his interim tag and giving him a three-year contract to continue as manager. Now he’ll look to accomplish what his predecessor Alex Cora couldn’t last year: beating the Yankees on the road in the AL Wild Card Series.
Boston has cooled off since going 32-5 to put itself in playoff position and faces some injury uncertainty going into October. Ceddanne Rafaela returned Tuesday after missing 16 games with a quad injury, and Willson Contreras was hit by a pitch on his right hand last Thursday and is dealing with soreness. On the mound, the Red Sox could receive two significant reinforcements for the bullpen in Garrett Crochet and Tanner Houck. Crochet, last season’s AL Cy Young runner-up, has been out with a shoulder injury since late April, while Houck hasn’t appeared in a game in 2026. -- Castillo
10. Cleveland Guardians
Record: 82-76
Previous ranking: 12
Cleveland is, once again, showing its knack for a strong finishing kick. Over the past decade, only the Dodgers have won more September games. For Guardians fans aching for their team’s first title since the Truman administration, October is a higher priority at this point.
Like the White Sox, the first order of business is to secure the AL Central title and the first-round bye likely to go with it. Given the neck-and-neck nature of Cleveland’s battle with Chicago, there likely isn’t going to be much time for manager Stephen Vogt to ease up on the pedal to finish the season. That would be nice to do when it comes to rookie ace Parker Messick, who will finish the season with at least 50 more innings than he has ever thrown in a season. Messick has shown no signs of fatigue, so it may not matter. -- Doolittle
11. Arizona Diamondbacks
Record: 84-74
Previous ranking: 10
Manager Torey Lovullo’s comments in a radio interview last week in which he acknowledged that the Diamondbacks “probably” -- his word -- need to reach the postseason to earn him a contract extension surprised many in the industry, as Lovullo has a strong and long-standing relationship with his boss, Mike Hazen. The Ketel Marte situation has been challenging for the organization, with the team’s highest-paid position player failing to show up to the park, and owner Ken Kendrick has a reputation for being mercurial and demanding. Lovullo’s contract runs out at season’s end, and he and the Diamondbacks agreed they would discuss his status then. -- Olney
12. Chicago White Sox
Record: 81-77
Previous ranking: 11
The White Sox have wobbled down the stretch, but they have not fallen down. It looks like they will join the playoff party, completing an incredible two-year turnaround that saw them go from setting the modern single-season loss record to playing in October.
Barring a face-plant over the last few days of the season, the question of whether the Sox can overtake Cleveland for the AL Central title is the biggest remaining question. It’s impactful, with a first-round bye likely on the line. A bye is a boon for any team, but among likely postseason entrants, it might loom largest for the White Sox. That’s just because of how manager Will Venable has had to stretch his pitching resources to the maximum just to get to this point. A wild-card skip would give his staff at least a little time to regroup before the ALDS begins. -- Doolittle
13. Pittsburgh Pirates
Record: 80-78
Previous ranking: 14
Why did Paul Skenes lapse into baseball’s pitching middle class rather than continue his march toward Cooperstown? There is no bigger task for the Pirates and Skenes this offseason than figuring this out. With one more start to go, he has already allowed more runs this season than he did in his first two seasons combined. To be sure, it’s not all on Skenes, whose expected ERA, 3.27 per Statcast, is unusually divergent from his actual ERA (3.91). Still, even a 3.27 ERA is a far cry from the level of effectiveness Skenes flashed before this season. Why? Finding the answer to that question could prove to be the biggest addition Pittsburgh makes this winter. -- Doolittle
14. Texas Rangers
Record: 78-80
Previous ranking: 16
With eyes on the disappointing Mariners and Yordan Alvarez’s Triple Crown watch, the Rangers quietly remained in contention in the historically dreadful AL West all summer. Following three straight losses, they now find themselves tied atop the division with Houston. Texas will host the Mets in a series finale Thursday before finishing the season with three games in Minnesota. The Rangers will need to finish with a better record than the Astros, who own the tiebreaker, to reach the postseason for the first time since winning the 2023 World Series. -- Castillo
15. Houston Astros
Record: 78-80
Previous ranking: 13
The Astros fired general manager Dana Brown last month and are under .500 with four games remaining ... but they still have a real chance to win the division. That’s the AL West in 2026. The Astros finish the regular season with a four-game series in West Sacramento against an A’s team that has an MLB-worst run differential. The bad news: The Astros head there tied atop the division. The good news: They hold the tiebreaker over Texas. In the background over the last few days of the season: Alvarez’s push to become the first player to win a Triple Crown since Miguel Cabrera in 2013. -- Castillo
16. Toronto Blue Jays
Record: 77-82
Previous ranking: 15
The Blue Jays did not replicate their 2025 magic in 2026, largely due to injuries and their offense falling off a cliff. They finished last season fourth in the majors with a 112 wRC+; this season, they’re tied for 24th with a 95 wRC+. The dropoff starts with Vladimir Guerrero Jr. and George Springer. Guerrero has nine home runs -- and, inexplicably, just one at home -- with a .695 OPS in the first year of a 14-year, $500 million contract extension. Springer, who reversed a precipitous decline to hit 32 home runs with a .959 OPS last season, has 15 home runs with a .730 OPS in 124 games this year -- and he’s a free agent after this season. Whether Springer re-signs or not, a rebound in 2027 starts with Guerrero sparking an offense that is tied for last in home runs in 2026. -- Castillo
17. Miami Marlins
Record: 78-80
Previous ranking: 18
Here’s the good news about the Marlins’ 2026 season: They hung around all year, battling among the contenders and having some individual successes. Here’s what’s not-so-great about where they stand right now: It’s hard to identify the players who could lead a Miami breakout into full-scale contention with the best NL teams.
Otto Lopez had an excellent season, but he’ll turn 28 years old next week and his OPS is under .800. Griffin Conine is the one player on the team with an OPS over .800, and he’s 29. Sandy Alcantara reestablished himself as a rotation leader, but he’s 31. Eury Perez has flashes of dominance and is just 23, but he’s got an injury history and will finish this season with an ERA over 4.00. More depth and more talent is needed for the Marlins to take the next step. -- Olney
18. Baltimore Orioles
Record: 78-81
Previous ranking: 19
Another disappointing season in Baltimore has already prompted some changes in the front office, but not at the top. President of baseball operations Mike Elias is expected to return in 2027. One move his front office got right was signing Pete Alonso last winter. The first baseman, who has played in every game this season, hit his 40th home run of the season in Monday’s win over the Blue Jays. He clearly isn’t why the Orioles aren’t going to the postseason for the second straight year.
Baltimore’s young position player core has not lived up to the hype, while the pitching staff wasn’t good enough to shoulder the load. Elias & Co. already decided to move on from former No. 1 pick Adley Rutschman, an All-Star catcher previously considered a foundational player, at the trade deadline. More significant moves could come this offseason. -- Castillo
19. St. Louis Cardinals
Record: 77-81
Previous ranking: 17
This rebuilding season has been an unqualified success for the Cardinals. If not for a leaky bullpen, their soft wild-card contention might have been a lot more solid. While bullpens are sometimes the final piece of the contention puzzle for a building team, that’s not always the case. Some clubs develop a bullpen-building process that takes effect even as the rest of the roster remains a work in progress. The Pirates of recent vintage are a good example.
Thus, the project of putting together a contention-worthy bullpen is a crucial one for the Chaim Bloom-led front office. Bloom was part of a Rays front office that annually churned out elite, no-name bullpens. However, during the four years that Bloom led the Red Sox front office, Boston ranked 24th in bullpen ERA (4.48) and middle-of-the-pack in save percentage. Good first year, but there is more to prove in St. Louis. -- Doolittle
20. Detroit Tigers
Record: 74-85
Previous ranking: 20
The Tigers will probably finish fourth in the AL in run differential, perhaps third if they pass the Red Sox, and will easily pace the Central by that measure. When you consider that, along with Detroit’s freakishly bad record in one- and two-run games (now 21-51) and the relatively short list of players on expiring deals (Jack Flaherty and Gleyber Torres, along with the retiring Justin Verlander), the Tigers are an obvious and very strong bounce-back candidate for the 2027 season. That doesn’t mean that president of baseball operations Scott Harris and his staff don’t have their work cut out for them when it comes to evaluating this lackluster season. Still, for the Tigers’ disappointed fans, it’s important to keep in mind that their team will be proceeding from a relative position of strength. -- Doolittle
21. Washington Nationals
Record: 75-84
Previous ranking: 23
In so many ways, the 2026 season was a success for the Nationals, who exceeded expectations this year, flirting with contention in the first half and seeing the development of players like CJ Abrams and James Wood into offensive stars. But the team’s pitching collapsed in the second half -- Washington’s second-half ERA of 4.49 ranks 25th. The Nationals locked down Cade Cavalli to a multiyear deal last week at the end of what has been a breakout season, but it’s clear that president of baseball operations Paul Toboni’s greatest challenge is to develop the sort of pipeline of pitching that will allow them to compete with the big-market teams in the division. -- Olney
22. Seattle Mariners
Record: 74-84
Previous ranking: 24
A year after falling one win short of the franchise’s first World Series appearance, the Mariners’ season will end Sunday with a whimper. The 2026 campaign will be remembered as the most disappointing one in franchise history.
Cal Raleigh’s drop-off from 60 home runs and an MVP runner-up finish was baffling. Julio Rodriguez regressed and still hasn’t made the superstar jump widely expected of him. Josh Naylor was a below-average hitter in the first year of his five-year contract. The starting rotation was not as good as advertised. Changes are inevitable, likely starting with manager Dan Wilson. But the Mariners can’t fire all of their players. They’ll need their core to bounce back from down seasons in order to rebound in 2027. -- Castillo
23. New York Mets
Record: 73-85
Previous ranking: 21
No one will go into the 2027 season under more pressure than David Stearns, the Mets’ head of baseball operations, following their collapse down the stretch in 2025 and the poor 2026 season. So it makes sense that he worked to keep someone he has a working relationship with in the managerial role, Andy Green, who had his interim tag removed and was hired to a three-year deal Tuesday. Steve Cohen’s comments on an SNY broadcast about needing new voices within the organization got the attention of a lot of rival executives, who wondered if the impact of Pete Alonso’s encore performance at Citi Field and the “Fire Stearns” chants last week made an impression on the owner. Under the circumstances, hiring Green seems like the right move for Stearns, the smart move. -- Olney
24. Minnesota Twins
Record: 75-84
Previous ranking: 22
The arrival of prospects Kaelen Culpepper, Walker Jenkins and Emmanuel Rodriguez has the Twins’ prospective 2027 position group in good shape even if veteran Josh Bell declines his mutual option and departs. The murkiest position is catcher, where Ryan Jeffers is likely headed for free agency, presumably after the Twins issue him a qualifying offer. The QO could limit Jeffers’ market, but probably not that much, as Jeffers looks like the best free agent catcher option out there. If he leaves, the Twins will need someone to pair with Caratini.
Long term, after drafting Vahn Lackey third in the most recent draft, the Twins seem in good shape with him, Eduardo Tait, Khadim Diaw and Carson Tinney all showing well in prospect rankings. Alas, none of that quartet is likely to be a 2027 solution. -- Doolittle
25. Cincinnati Reds
Record: 73-85
Previous ranking: 25
The ongoing maturation of Elly De La Cruz, as he edges toward his career prime, has provided ample reason to keep an eye on the Reds, even amid a last-place showing. Still, there have been enough trade rumors regarding the supremely talented shortstop to make you wonder just how long De La Cruz will be around.
Recent comments made by his agent, Scott Boras, don’t help. Boras suggested to reporters that a future foray into the open market made more sense for De La Cruz than a below-market extension. What does that mean for the Reds in the near term? For now, he has three more years of team control, so there’s no reason to be rash. Still, with this cloud starting to form over Great American Park, some sort of clarity about how the Reds plan to deal with their best player would be nice. -- Doolittle
26. Kansas City Royals
Record: 68-90
Previous ranking: 26
The Royals’ biggest offseason project will be to figure out their 2027 bullpen formula. That process begins with evaluating the relievers already on hand. Presumed closer Carlos Estevez had shoulder surgery -- bafflingly not until the second week of September -- and the Royals almost certainly won’t pick up their 2027 club option on him. Lucas Erceg looked lost before being shipped off to Omaha, but he performed well in Triple-A and his velocity upon his return to the majors has been at its highest level all year. Which Erceg is the real one? Is journeyman righty Nate Pearson a leverage option? Does Craig Kimbrel have anything left? The Royals will need relief help from outside the organization, but how much of it will depend on the outcome of these evaluations and others. -- Doolittle
27. San Francisco Giants
Record: 65-94
Previous ranking: 27
The general perception of San Francisco’s farm system is that it improved in 2026, and Bryce Eldridge established himself as a player the organization could build around. Beyond that, however, the Giants really haven’t progressed. They have a top-heavy payroll situation, with hundreds of millions owed to Rafael Devers, Willy Adames and Matt Chapman. The questions about manager Tony Vitello making the jump from college to professional baseball weren’t quelled by his first season with the Giants -- and neither were the questions about the man who hired him, Buster Posey, who is still relatively new to his front office role. -- Olney
28. Athletics
Record: 63-95
Previous ranking: 28
The A’s are stumbling to the finish line having lost 95 games. All-Star catcher Shea Langeliers recently returned from knee surgery, but several other prominent players remain on the IL, including Nick Kurtz, Tyler Soderstrom, Jacob Wilson, Brent Rooker, Luis Severino and Gage Jump. They’ll enter their season-ending series against the Astros with a negative-217 run differential -- the worst in the majors by 33 runs. With one season remaining before the A’s move to Las Vegas in 2028, they enter the winter in search of a general manager after David Forst’s departure in early August. Their offseason priorities are straightforward: Get healthy and improve a pitching staff that has a 5.43 ERA (29th) despite pitching half its games at the launchpad known as Sutter Health Park. -- Castillo
29. Los Angeles Angels
Record: 60-98
Previous ranking: 29
The Angels, despite 11 straight losing seasons, are the only franchise in the majors that has yet to post a 100-loss season. That could change this weekend in Seattle, where the Angels will need to win three of four games to avoid reaching the century mark. It’d be a fitting conclusion to Arte Moreno’s tenure as owner. Last month, Moreno agreed to sell controlling interest in the team to Stan Kroenke for a record valuation of $4 billion. Kroenke will take over a franchise that has not appeared in the postseason since 2014 and has not won a postseason game since 2009.
The first order of business this offseason will be hiring fired general manager Perry Minasian’s replacement. The team could also be in search of a manager to replace Kurt Suzuki, who is on a one-year contract. It is a transformative time in Anaheim. -- Castillo
30. Colorado Rockies
Record: 57-101
Previous ranking: 30
Colorado has compiled 100 losses for the fourth consecutive season; the last team to suffer 100-plus losses in five consecutive seasons were the Phillies, from 1938 to 1942. In Paul DePodesta’s first year of running Colorado’s baseball operations, there were some under-the-hood improvements: the biggest run differential improvement of all 30 teams in 2026, an improved farm system and some nice finds for the every-day lineup, like Jake McCarthy, TJ Rumfield and Connor Norby. There’s still a long way to go to competitive relevance for the Rockies, especially given the high bar required in the Dodgers’ NL West. -- Olney

item.content:encoded:
Every Monday, this column will break down the most popular waiver wire and free agent acquisitions from the weekend. I dig into the top adds on the ever-popular Fantrax and in the NFBC Online Championship (OC), a national mid-stakes contest with 240 total leagues of 12 and a six-figure grand prize. Reviewing player adds between the two should provide us with a well-rounded perspective and barometer of the fantasy baseball marketplace.
Week 26 Overview
Hitters
The San Diego Padres took advantage of their four-game series with the Rockies at Coors Field and a home set with the Marlins, scoring 51 runs, 12 more than any other team. Fernando Tatis Jr. (along with Brandon Lowe and Pete Crow-Armstrong) led the way with a week-high four dingers. Last week’s streamers turned out to be dynamite: Jake Cronenworth (.464-8-2-8-2), Dustin Harris (.379-5-0-7-2) and Samad Taylor (.556-6-1-7-1) really stepped up, particularly Taylor for my competitive Main Event squad that gained two category points in batting average last week. Rake Cronenworth was true to his nickname from several years ago. He led all Major League hitters with 13 hits. The Brewers swiped a league-high 12 bags last week: four each for Jackson Chourio and rookie Cooper Pratt. Tampa’s Chandler Simpson led all runners with five swipes, finally catching Washington’s Nasim Nuñez for the MLB lead with 46. Expect Simpson to finish with 50+ and win the stolen base crown.
Pitchers
Of the 29 two-start pitchers excluding Pirates opener Lake Bachar, three earned two wins: Tarik Skubal, Sean Burke and David Peterson. Houston’s Hunter Brown had an outstanding two-step (10 IP – 5 H – 1 ER – 5 K – 20 K) and those 20 punchouts led all pitchers for the week. Gavin Williams punched out 16 in 12 innings and is back atop the AL lead in strikeouts with 244. Dylan Cease (239) may not make his final start of the season and Cam Schlittler (234) is unlikely to catch Williams as both have one start remaining. It’s very possible that Williams catches and passes Jacob Misiorowski (247) for the Major League lead. The Miz pitched three innings in his weekend start and might be limited for his final one.
Tampa’s Bryan Baker was the first reliever to reach 40 saves this season. It’s possible that Cade Smith (39), Riley O’Brien (38) and Mason Miller (37) join Baker. The last time there were three closers with 40 or more saves was in 2019: Edwin Díaz (57), Wade Davis (43), and Craig Kimbrel (42). Shout out to folks who drafted O’Brien late, and/or picked up Baker, Louis Varland or Jacob Latz off waivers and didn’t have to worry about the saves category all season.
Week 27 Most Added Players: NFBC Main Event, NFBC OC, and Fantrax
It’s the last hurrah for managers with FAB dollars left, hoping to get the best bang for the buck and for variance to lean their way and tip them into league titles. As is usually the case in the final week, we hope to optimize our pitching rotations and hitters in hitter-friendly ballparks against bad pitching. It was odd seeing Shohei Ohtani available in several leagues, and perhaps fortuitous as he should be activated this week and start a few games. Ohtani was acquired in 26 OCs for an AWB of $17. In Main Events, there were 12 shares available and they went for a reasonable $12 a pop. I scooped up a rare Ohtani share in an OC for $2, winning a tiebreaker over the team in 1st place in that league. Andy Pages will be activated on Tuesday, which should push Tommy Edman back to second base. Pages had been out since August 21, but was producing at an exciting clip before the injury — .272 – 72 R – 21 HR – 80 RBI – 12 SB in 550 PA. Managers who acquired him are hoping that he dusts the cobwebs back off and gets right into the swing of things, with all the marbles on the line.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Andy Pages | LAD | OF | 60% | $5 |
| 2 | JR Ritchie | ATL | SP | 57% | $3 |

| 5 | Jose Siri | LAA | OF | 45% | $4 |
| 6 | Heliot Ramos | NYY | OF | 35% | $7 |
| 7 | Dansby Swanson | CHC | SS | 35% | $8 |
| 8 | Brayan Bello | BOS | SP | 35% | $11 |
| 9 | Dustin Harris | SD | OF | 32% | $10 |
| 10 | Garrett Whitlock | BOS | RP | 32% | $5 |
| 11 | Pavin Smith | ARI | 1B | 30% | $4 |
| 12 | Anthony Volpe | NYY | SS | 30% | $5 |
AWB = Average Winning Bid (min: $4 AWB)
Pitchers were the most popular targets, specifically two-steppers, as we chase wins and strikeouts, hoping the Ratio Monster doesn’t eat our leads in ERA and WHIP. JR Ritchie and Daniel Lynch IV were the most added starters who we expect two starts from this week. Ritchie’s MLB debut back in April came with great promise, but walks haunted him greatly, which led to trips back to Triple-A to refine his craft and some bulk inning relief work when he returned to Atlanta in July. Ritchie was recently promoted again, and ran into a juggernaut Cubs offense last week, allowing six runs on seven hits in 4.2 innings. The walk rate (13.7%) isn’t pretty, and he has a good opportunity to end his season on a high note with two reasonable matchups — against the Reds at home and the Marlins on the road. Lynch had served the Royals well as their top southpaw out of the bullpen for most of the season. He moved to the rotation in August and slowly worked his pitch counts upward. Lynch has made it to five innings in each of his last three starts. His latest one (at HOU on September 16) went well — 5 IP – 2 H – 0 ER – 1 BB – 3 K. More of that please as he faces the White Sox and Guardians at Kauffman Stadium in the final week. If I could only choose one for the week, it would be Ritchie.
Red Sox pitchers Brayan Bello and Garrett Whitlock were popular buys as the likelihood of roto stars shining bright on them this week is high. Bello is coming off a tremendous outing against the AL-leading Rays on Saturday where he posted an 11:0 K:BB with just one run allowed in eight innings. Those 11 punchies tied his career high. Bello had been the worst starter in the game (6.49 ERA, 1.67 WHIP) through June 4, when he was optioned to Triple-A. Since the All-Star break, mostly out of relief and with two starts, the 27-year-old has been shining. Over those 51.1 innings, he is rocking exemplary ratios (2.28 ERA, 1.01 WHIP) and a 17% K-BB% (22.3% K, 5.3% BB). Bello should make a start against the Cubs next Saturday. The Cubs should be settled into a playoff spot by then, so perhaps they give Pete Crow-Armstrong and some of the other regulars that day off. Boston’s closer Aroldis Chapman has been day-to-day with a lat issue, so perhaps the Red sox have him take it easy and provide Whitlock with some save opportunities. Whitlock has a 7-2 record with a 17.5 ERA, 0.88 WHIP and four saves.
Streaming Diamondbacks is a good idea this week, specifically for their three-game set at Coors Field against the Rockies in the early part of the week. Pavin Smith was a coveted target, coming off a four-day stretch where three of his hits were home runs. Don’t expect Smith to start against lefty Kyle Freeland, but he should be in the lineup for the other two contests against righties. Nolan Arenado was available in one of the 60 Main Event leagues and was acquired for just one dollar.
Better late than never for two punchless Padres who have been quite productive and certainly enjoyed their visit to Coors Field in the first half of last week. Dustin Harris ($10 AWB) and Samad Taylor ($5) have been red hot and playing often over the last 10 days. Though he doesn’t have a home run yet, Harris has been quite productive and helpful to early-bird managers: eight runs, 12 runs batted in and three steals, batting .384 with a 166 wRC+ in 40 plate appearances since September 11. He’s also been batting second against right-handed starters. Taylor has at least one hit in nine of his last 10, including a 3-for-3 effort on Sunday, and has driven in seven in his last seven games.

As always, more reliable starting pitcher depth was available in the 12-team OC pool. Cristian Javier, Anthony Kay, Robert Gasser, Lynch, Yusei Kikuchi, and Max Scherzer were the most added pitchers this week. Javier should pitch twice this week and will hope to put his best foot forward (in this case, his right arm) as the Astros fight for the AL West and a playoff spot. Sutter Health Park is not a fun place to pitch, but the A’s lineup is a watered-down version without Brent Rooker, Nick Kurtz, Tyler Soderstrom, and Jacob Wilson윌슨. Javier’s first start is in Seattle may not be a picnic with gluten-free granola and Pearl Jam on the Discman.
Milwaukee’s Robert Gasser only draws one start (home vs. STL), but is considered a reliable ratios guy who can score a much-needed win for fantasy managers, as the Brewers will certainly be favorites in that matchup. Gasser earned his fifth win on Saturday, throwing seven scoreless innings against the Orioles. White Sox lefty Anthony Kay has good matchups (at KC on Tuesday and vs. COL on Sunday), though that second start could be pulled away from him. The main problems here is that Kay hasn’t made it to the fifth inning in any of his last five starts. I feel much more comfortable with a single start against the Orioles from Max Scherzer than I do a double (at SEA, at ATH) from wily Yusei Kikuchi. Kikuchi has walked 12 batters in his last three starts.

It’s possible that attraction towards Ryan Johnson this weekend relates to dynasty and keeper formats, and not his start in Seattle this week. Johnson has limited run damage over his last nine starts, since August 6, posting a 2.39 ERA, but with an xFIP (5.01) nearly double the mark. Johnson is more of a 4.25-4.50 ERA guy than a sub-3.00 ERA one, as his 90.9% LOB and .229 BABIP portends.
Perhaps a similar mindset applies to folks who scooped up Jack Perkins, who pitched two quality starts on the road against the Rays (6.2 IP – 4 H – 0 ER – 1 BB – 8 K) and the Guardians (6 IP – 5 H – 1 ER – 0 BB – 4 K), flashing some of his upside and future potential. Perkins has had a difficult season (5.90 ERA, but a 4.16 xFIP, 1.45 WHIP) and will be a tough streamer at home in Sacramento next season, but the strikeouts (25.2%) should always be there.
Andrew Alvarez should have a rotation spot with the Nationals next season. He has been outstanding since the All-Star break, posting a 2.44 ERA (3.30 FIP, 4.02 xFIP) with a 1.10 WHIP and a 22.7% strikeout rate, though he wasn’t able to secure a win in any of those 10 starts. Alvarez won’t be a particularly coveted target in drafts next season, but should have a NFBC ADP somewhere in the 250-325 overall range. He may be a consideration in NL-only keeper leagues with deep benches and five-plus keepers.
Bold Predictions for Week 27
Gavin Williams and Jacob Misiorowski finish the season tied for the MLB lead in strikeouts with 255. Williams punches out 11 and Misiorowski, eight.
JR Ritchie steps up for his two starts and has a Jack Perkins Week 26 type week, helping managers win league titles.
Cade Cavalli twirls a gem in Detroit this week and pulls his 3.02 ERA under 3.00 to end the season. Cavalli will have a top-60 ADP in 2027.
Jo Adell takes advantage of four left-handed starters this week and earns seven RBIs to reach 100, after falling two RBIs short last season.
One of Cristian Javier or Yusei Kikuchi will remind why streaming pitchers in Sutter Health Park, even if part of a two-step, is a mistake.
Miguel Vargas and Colson Montgomery hit three home runs each this week and the White Sox score the most runs in Week 27.
The Houston Astros win the NL West and knock the Texas Rangers out of playoff contention.
I hope you enjoyed my column this season and that you found it helpful, or at least entertaining and informative. Stay tuned for more from me next week as we hit the offseason streets. Best of luck this final week!
